To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the commonly used NO trapping method based on the Fe(2+) dithiocarbamato complex can lead to erroneous results because of complex redox chemistry of these complexes.
the commonly used iron-dithiocarbonate complexes and their NO adducts exhibit complex redox behavior, which should be considered for the use of these complexes as NO traps.
iron-dithiocarabmate complexes and their NO adducts are redox active and undergo reversible oxidation and reduction.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new method for the detection of NO in the presence of oxygen.
the chemistry of nitric oxide and its reaction with metal complexes.
the development of novel methods for trapping and detection of NO and its derivatives in biological systems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of the Fe(3+)(dithiocarbamato)-complexes to estimate NO levels in biological systems may lead to erroneous estimates of NO generation.

the Fe(2+) dithiocarbamato complexes are suitable NO-traps only when the reaction with NO is carried out under anaerobic conditions and when the excess of the Fe(2+)/Fe(3+) ratio in the reaction mixture is high.
the Fe-dithiocarbamatess are not suitable for quantitative NO measurements in biological systems.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Fe(3+) derivatives of MGD and DETC are formed rapidly under aerobic conditions and are not suitable for the detection of NO in vivo.
NO-Fe(II)-DETC is more suitable for NO trapping and NO-Fe (III)-MGD for NO detection.
the Fe(2+) complex of MGD is oxidized in the presence of oxygen, forming the Fe(3+) complex.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the NO-Fe-dithiocarbamide complexes are redox sensitive and can undergo complex redoxic reactions that can lead to under or overestimation of the NO concentration in biological systems.
Fe(2+), Fe(3+) and NO-Fe complexes of iron-dithiocabamates undergo complex redox reactions in aqueous solutions.
the Fe(3+)(NO)-dithiocarabmate complexes are not stable in biological systems and they are rapidly reduced to Fe(2)(NO) complexes.
